analysis.one_liner: Lets employers ban union organizing and picketing from their property, even while hosting charities.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 57 cosponsors and one hearing, it sat in committee until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so that no employer has to let employees, union organizers, or picketers onto its business property for union activity. That would stay true even if the same employer opens its doors to charities, civic groups, or churches. In practice, it would remove one of the few places — the workplace itself — where union organizing has legal protection.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially those with customer-facing or large properties (retail, hospitality, manufacturing sites), gain the clear legal right to keep union organizers, solicitors, and picketers off their premises without facing an unfair-labor-practice case.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers, especially retail and property owners

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 8(a)(1) of the National Labor Relations Act to state that an employer is not required to allow access to its business property for union organizing, solicitation, distribution, or picketing [S2][S3].
The exemption applies even when the employer allows access to charitable, civic, or religious organizations, so the bill targets union advocacy specifically [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to organize a union and the unions that represent them lose access to the workplace — historically the most effective venue for reaching employees — making union campaigns harder and more expensive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers trying to organize and their unions

drawbacks.text: It strips employees and organizers of access to the one place where co-workers can most easily be reached, weakening workers' ability to form unions and bargain collectively [S2][S3].
The rule is one-sided: an employer could welcome charities and civic groups onto the property but bar union advocates, putting union speech on a lower footing than other speech [S2][S3].

A good-faith defense of the bill is private property rights — that owners should decide who advocates on their premises. The counter-cost is that union organizing has almost no practical substitute for workplace access.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Employers get a clearer property-rights shield, but the bill buys that by singling out union activity for exclusion — including by employers who welcome charities — and shifting an already uneven playing field further toward management. For ordinary workers, the costs outweigh the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House committee and a subcommittee, got one hearing in February 1996, and was never voted out of committee before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Hoekstra introduced the bill on October 18, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities [S5].
It was sent to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations on November 3, 1995 [S5].
The committee held a hearing on February 7, 1996, but no markup or floor vote ever followed, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5][S1].
The bill drew 57 cosponsors — 55 Republicans and 2 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: no new access rules passed, so they keep the practical advantage they already hold over workplace organizing. Union organizers were spared a new legal handicap they would have carried indefinitely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; union organizers were spared a handicap

for.name: Rep. Peter Hoekstra
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to amend the National Labor Relations Act's property-access rules

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.role: Committee of referral; controlled by the Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing on February 7, 1996, but never reported the bill or scheduled a vote

against.name: Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on November 3, 1995; took no further recorded action

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican: 55 of the 57 cosponsors were Republicans, with 2 Democrats; the bill died in a committee run by the Republican majority without a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Employers (retail, hospitality, manufacturing and other property owners)
industries.note: The bill would give employers a clear legal right to bar union organizing, solicitation, and picketing from their property, removing a check on their control of the workplace. Workers' organizing power depends heavily on that access.

Unions would lose legal protection for the workplace access that organizing drives rely on, making campaigns costlier and less likely to succeed. Their interest runs with the workers they seek to represent.
